explanations.answer: Silence for about half an hour
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. "When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour." After six seals and all that noise, heaven goes quiet. I'd have checked whether my ears were still working.

explanations.answer: A new song before the throne
explanations.explanation: A new song does show up in Revelation, but earlier. In Revelation 5:9, they sing it when the Lamb takes the scroll. At the seventh seal, the text gives us silence in heaven for about half an hour. No music, not even humming.

explanations.answer: A sound like a mighty wind
explanations.explanation: A sound like a rushing wind does happen in the Bible, but in Acts 2:2, when a sound comes from heaven. Here, the seventh seal brings the opposite of a sound. The text says there was silence in heaven for about half an hour. I'd say the wind took the day off.

explanations.answer: The prayers of all the saints
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The angel is given much incense to offer, "along with the prayers of all the saints, on the golden altar before the throne." Those prayers aren't tucked in a corner. They're right there with the incense at the altar before the throne. I think that's worth a slow, happy nod.

explanations.answer: The crowns of all the elders
explanations.explanation: Crowns do get laid down before the throne in Revelation 4:10, where the elders cast theirs down. That's a different moment. In this scene, the angel offers incense along with the prayers of all the saints. The crowns stay out of this one.

explanations.answer: The palm branches of the crowd
explanations.explanation: Palm branches belong to Revelation 7:9, where a great multitude stands before the throne holding them. Here the text puts something else on the altar with the incense. It's the prayers of all the saints. Nobody's waving a branch at this altar.

Not quite, baker, and I'm glad the text is clear on this one. It says the smoke and the prayers “…rose up before God from the hand of the angel.” They don't fade away on the trip. They rise up before God. I'd hold on to that line.

That's right. The text says the smoke of the incense, together with the prayers of the saints, “…rose up before God from the hand of the angel.” Nothing fades on the way. The prayers go up from the angel's hand and arrive before God.

You've got it. The angel took the censer, filled it with fire from the altar, and “…hurled it to the earth…” That's not a gentle toss. It lands with thunder, lightning and an earthquake, and the text says all of that in one breath.

The incense and the prayers are before the throne, but the censer doesn't stay there. The angel fills it with fire from the altar and “…hurled it to the earth…” So the fire travels down, not up. Nobody sets this one down gently.

I can see why you'd think of the Lamb, since He's the one who opened the seventh seal. But the text doesn't have the angel hand the censer to anyone. He fills it with fire from the altar and “…hurled it to the earth…” That's the action in this verse.

True, and the text packs it all in. When the censer is hurled to the earth, there are "peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake." That's sound, light and shaking, all at once. I'd have grabbed the counter.

This one is true, friend. The text says that after the censer is hurled to the earth, "there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake." Nothing in that list gets skipped. I'd have grabbed the counter too.

explanations.answer: Hail and fire mixed with blood
explanations.explanation: That's the one. When the first angel sounded his trumpet, "hail and fire mixed with blood were hurled down upon the earth." Hail and fire don't usually travel together, and the text adds blood on top. It's a heavy picture, and the text doesn't soften it.

Fire from heaven is familiar, and sulfur and fire fell on Sodom in Genesis 19:24. But this trumpet doesn't bring sulfur. The text says hail and fire mixed with blood were hurled down upon the earth. Same sky, different list.

Those are from Egypt, in the plagues in Exodus 8. Different story, different crowd. At this trumpet, the text says hail and fire mixed with blood were hurled down upon the earth. Not a single frog in the verse.

Yes, baker. "A third of the earth was burned up, along with a third of the trees and all the green grass." Hail and fire were hurled down, and the fire does its work. I've burned a batch or two myself, but never a third of the earth.

Washed sounds almost gentle, and nothing here is gentle. The text says hail and fire mixed with blood were hurled down, and "a third of the earth was burned up." That's fire, not a rinse. Washing is a job for a sink.

Swept makes me think of a clean floor, and this is the opposite. After hail and fire mixed with blood come down, the text says "a third of the earth was burned up." The word is burned. A broom wouldn't be much help.
True. Look at the wording: a third of the earth and a third of the trees, then "all the green grass." Most of the list says a third, but the grass says all. Good eye, baker.

This one is true, friend, and the wording is easy to blur. The text says "A third of the earth was burned up, along with a third of the trees and all the green grass." The earth and the trees get a third, but the green grass gets all. That one word changes it.

explanations.answer: A third of them are destroyed
explanations.explanation: Right on the money. The text says "a third of the ships were destroyed." It comes right after a third of the sea turns to blood and a third of the living creatures in the sea die. That number keeps showing up, and you caught it.

explanations.answer: All of them turn back to port
explanations.explanation: Turning back to port is a sensible plan, but the text doesn't mention it. It says "a third of the ships were destroyed." Nothing in the verse says the ships turn around.

Half is close to a third, but the text uses the number third. It says "a third of the ships were destroyed." And the verse says destroyed, not run aground. I'd stick with the exact numbers on this one.

Not this time, baker. The text says that when the sea turned to blood, "a third of the living creatures in the sea died." So not every creature survives. This part is heavy, and the text just says it plainly.

You've got it. With the second trumpet, the text says "a third of the living creatures in the sea died." So the claim that every one survives doesn't match what the text says. It's a heavy line, and I won't pretend it isn't.
Not quite, friend, and this one is heavy. The text says "many people died from the bitter waters." So the bitter waters do harm people. I think this is a verse to read slowly.

That's right. The text says a third of the waters turned bitter, and "many people died from the bitter waters." So the claim that no one is harmed doesn't match the verse. It's a hard line, and I think it deserves a quiet moment.

explanations.answer: A third of day and night go dark
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. "A third of the stars were darkened, a third of the day was without light, and a third of the night as well." The light drops by a third, day and night. That's a lot of dimmer switch.

explanations.answer: The sun stands still in the sky
explanations.explanation: The sun does stand still in the Bible, in Joshua 10:13, with Joshua, Israel's leader. That's a different story. Here the fourth trumpet strikes a third of the sun and moon and stars. A third of the day and a third of the night go without light.

explanations.answer: The sky rolls up like a scroll
explanations.explanation: That picture is in Revelation 6:14, when the sky recedes like a scroll being rolled up. It belongs to the sixth seal, not this trumpet. At the fourth trumpet, a third of the sun and moon and stars are struck. A third of the day is without light, and a third of the night as well.

explanations.answer: The trumpets of the last three angels
explanations.explanation: You've got it. The eagle cries, "Woe! Woe! Woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the trumpet blasts about to be sounded by the remaining three angels!" Four trumpets have sounded and three are left. That's the warning.

explanations.answer: A storm about to hit the seas
explanations.explanation: The seas did take a hit at the second trumpet, but that one has already happened. The eagle's warning is about something still coming. It cries woe "…because of the trumpet blasts about to be sounded by the remaining three angels!"

explanations.answer: A famine coming upon the land
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't name a famine here. The eagle flies overhead and cries woe "…because of the trumpet blasts about to be sounded by the remaining three angels!" The warning is about the three trumpets still waiting.
